questions.question: [NEET 2022 | Biology] A person with blood group AB can donate blood to:
questions.solution: # Blood Group AB Donation Compatibility ## **Correct Answer: (B) Only AB group** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### Understanding Blood Group AB: - **Antigens present on RBCs:** A and B - **Antibodies in plasma:** NONE (neither anti-A nor anti-B) ### Donation Compatibility Rule: When a person donates blood, the **donor's RBC antigens** must NOT react with the **recipient's plasma antibodies**. ### Checking Each Recipient Group: | Recipient | Antigens | Plasma Antibodies | AB Donor Compatible? | |-----------|----------|-------------------|----------------------| | **O** | None | Anti-A, Anti-B | \u₂₇₄c NO (B antigen will react) | | **A** | A | Anti-B | \u₂₇₄c NO (B antigen will react) | | **B** | B | Anti-A | \u₂₇₄c NO (A antigen will react) | | **AB** | A, B | NONE | \u₂₇₀₅ YES (no antibodies to react) | --- ## Key Concept: **Blood Group Compatibility:** - **AB = Universal RECIPIENT** (can receive from all groups) - **O = Universal DONOR** (can donate to all groups) - **AB = Most restricted DONOR** (can donate only to AB) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A)** Universal donor is O, not AB - **(C)** A recipients have anti-B antibodies that will attack AB donor's B antigens - **(D)** B recipients have anti-A antibodies that will attack AB donor's A antigens --- ## Remember: **AB blood group people are universal *recipients* but the most restricted *donors*\—they can only give to AB recipients!**

questions.question: [NEET 2016 | Biology] WRONG statement about gene I controlling ABO blood groups:

options.B: Person has only two of three alleles
options.D: Allele i is dominant over IA and IB

questions.solution: ## Answer: **(D) Allele i is dominant over IA and IB** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### Let me verify each statement: | Statement | Correct? | Why? | |-----------|----------|------| | (A) Gene I has 3 alleles | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | The alleles are: IA, IB, and i | | (B) Person has only 2 of 3 alleles | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | Humans are diploid; each person inherits 2 alleles only | | (C) IA and IB are codominant | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | IAIB genotype produces AB blood group (both expressed equally) | | (D) **i is dominant over IA and IB** | \u₂₇₁₇ **FALSE** | **i is actually RECESSIVE to both** | --- ## The Core Concept: ABO Blood Group Dominance **Correct dominance hierarchy:** - IA and IB are **codominant** to each other - Both IA and IB are **dominant** over i (recessive) **Genotype \u₂₁₉₂ Phenotype:** - IAIA or IAi \u₂₁₉₂ **A blood group** - IBIB or IBi \u₂₁₉₂ **B blood group** - IAIB \u₂₁₉₂ **AB blood group** - ii \u₂₁₉₂ **O blood group** Notice that in IAi and IBi, the recessive i allele is masked by the dominant alleles. This proves i is **recessive**, not dominant. --- ## Key Takeaway: **Remember:** The allele 'i' stands for "isoagglutinin-free" and is recessive to both IA and IB, which produce their respective antigens on red blood cells.

questions.question: Why 1st child of Rh+ husband and Rh− wife doesn’t have erythroblastosis foetalis?

options.A: Due to the absence of Rh antigen in mother’s blood
options.B: Due to the presence of Rh antibodies in mother’s blood
options.C: Due to the absence of Rh antibodies in mother’s blood

questions.solution: **Correct Answer: (C)** **Explanation:** Due to the absence of Rh antibodies in mother’s blood. A special case of Rh incompatibility has been observed between Rh −ve blood of pregnant mother with Rh +ve blood of foetus. During the delivery of the first child there is a possibility of exposure of the maternal blood to small amount of Rh +ve blood from foetus. In such cases, the mother starts preparing antibodies against Rh antigen in her blood. In the case of her subsequent pregnancies, the Rh antibody from the mother can leak to blood of foetus and destroy foetal RBC. This could be fatal to foetus or could cause severe anaemia and jaundice to the foetus. This condition in called erythroblastosis foetalis
